title: Psalms and Proverbs
bigQuestion: How do the songs and sayings in the Ketuvim put big feelings and big questions into words?

story.title: A Song About Green Pastures
story.kicker: The same six-verse song is sung softly at a bedside and out loud in a stadium full of people.
paragraphs: Leo's grandma is in the hospital in Chicago. She is tired, but she wants to hear a song. Leo's uncle takes out a small book. He reads slowly: "The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want." Grandma closes her eyes and smiles. She knows every word. She learned it as a girl.

The song is Psalm 23. It is only six verses long. It talks about green grass, quiet water and a dark valley. It says a shepherd walks with the sheep the whole way. Leo asks, "Why this song?" His uncle says, "Because it is about not being alone."

Two weeks later, Leo is at a big stadium with his class. Before the game, a singer walks to the middle of the field. She sings the same words. Thousands of people go quiet. Some sing along. Leo whispers, "That is Grandma's song!"

On the bus home, Leo's teacher explains. The Psalms are a book of 150 songs in the Hebrew Bible. Jewish tradition calls the book Tehillim, which means "praises." Some songs are happy. Some are sad. Some ask hard questions. People have sung them for more than two thousand years.
Leo thinks about that. One song for a hospital room and a stadium. One song for a grandma and a crowd. He decides he wants to learn the rest of the words.
story.think: Why do you think one short song can fit a quiet hospital room and a loud stadium at the same time?

lessons.title: Tehillim: 150 Songs
lessons.mainIdea: The book of Psalms is a collection of 150 songs and poems, and Jewish tradition calls it Tehillim, or praises.
reading: The *Ketuvim* are the third part of the Hebrew Bible. The word means "writings." The first book in the Ketuvim is the book of *Psalms*. In Hebrew it is called *Tehillim*. That means "praises." The book holds 150 songs and poems.

The Psalms are not one story. They are a songbook. Some psalms are short. Psalm 117 has only two verses. Some are long. Psalm 119 has 176 verses. Many psalms have a title at the top. The title of Psalm 23 says it is "a Psalm of David." Jewish tradition connects many psalms with King David.

People sing psalms in synagogues and homes. They say them when they are happy and when they are sad. Scholars say the psalms were written over many hundreds of years. Different writers added songs to the book. That is why it holds so many kinds of feelings.

words.d: the third part of the Hebrew Bible; the word means "writings"
the book of 150 songs and poems in the Hebrew Bible
the Hebrew name for the book of Psalms; it means "praises"

look.title: Short Songs and Long Songs
look.cite: The Holy Scriptures, Jewish Publication Society, 1917
look.prompt: Which psalm is the longest? Which is the shortest? How many times longer is the longest one than Psalm 23?

check.q: How many psalms are in the book of Psalms?
check.why: The book of Psalms holds 150 songs and poems. Twenty-four is the number of books in the whole Tanakh.

check.q: What does the Hebrew name Tehillim mean?
check.why: Tehillim means "praises." Ketuvim means "writings," and Torah means "teaching."

check.q: Which part of the Hebrew Bible holds the book of Psalms?
check.why: Psalms is the first book of the Ketuvim, the Writings. The Talmud is not part of the Hebrew Bible.

lessons.title: The Shepherd Song
lessons.mainIdea: Psalm 23 pictures God as a shepherd who stays with the sheep, and people have sung it for comfort for a very long time.
reading: Psalm 23 is one of the most famous songs in the world. It is very short. It begins, "The LORD is my shepherd." A *shepherd* takes care of sheep. A shepherd finds them grass and water. A shepherd walks with them through dark places and keeps them safe.

The psalm uses this picture for God. The singer says he is like a sheep. He is led to green fields and quiet water. Even in a dark valley he is not afraid. The psalm says the shepherd's rod and staff give *comfort*. Comfort means feeling calm and safe when something is hard.

Jewish families often sing Psalm 23 at the Shabbat table. Many people say it at a funeral or beside a sick person. Christians read it too. Jewish tradition and Christian tradition both treasure this song. Each reads it in its own way.

words.d: a person who takes care of sheep, finds them food and keeps them safe
the feeling of being calm and safe when something is hard

look.title: Psalm 23 Begins
look.text: The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want.
look.cite: Psalm 23:1, The Holy Scriptures, Jewish Publication Society, 1917
look.prompt: "I shall not want" means "I will not be missing anything I need." Why would a sheep with a good shepherd feel that way?

check.q: In Psalm 23, God is pictured as what?
check.why: Psalm 23 begins, "The LORD is my shepherd." The singer is like a sheep being led and kept safe.

check.q: What does "comfort" mean in this lesson?
choices: Feeling calm and safe when something is hard
check.why: Comfort is the feeling of being calm and safe during a hard time. The psalm says the shepherd's rod and staff bring comfort.

check.q: When do many Jewish families sing Psalm 23?
choices: Never; it is only read silently
check.why: Many Jewish families sing Psalm 23 at the Shabbat table. It is also said beside the sick and at funerals.

lessons.title: Songs of Thanks and Praise
lessons.mainIdea: Psalms like 100 and 150 tell everyone and everything to praise God with singing and music.
reading: Not every psalm is quiet. Some are loud and happy. Psalm 100 has only five verses. Its title calls it a song of thanksgiving. It tells all the earth to shout. It says to serve God with gladness and come with singing. The word for a glad shout is *praise*.

Psalm 150 is the last song in the book. It is like a big finish. It names many instruments: the horn, the harp, the drum, the flute and loud cymbals. Its last line says that everything that breathes should praise God. Then it ends with one word, *Hallelujah*. That means "praise the LORD."

Jewish tradition puts these psalms into daily prayer. Psalm 100 is said in the morning service on most days. Psalm 150 is said every morning too. So a Jewish child in Chicago may say these words before school. The psalms are very old, but people still sing them.

words.d: to say or sing that someone or something is great
a Hebrew word that means "praise the LORD"; it ends many psalms

look.title: The Last Line of the Book
look.text: The last verse of Psalm 150 says that everything that has breath should praise the LORD, and then it ends with the word Hallelujah.
look.cite: Psalm 150:6, The Holy Scriptures, Jewish Publication Society, 1917
look.prompt: Psalm 150 lists horns, harps, drums, flutes and cymbals. Why do you think the book of Psalms ends with such a loud song?

check.q: What does "Hallelujah" mean?
check.why: Hallelujah is a Hebrew word that means "praise the LORD." Psalm 150 ends with it.

check.q: Which psalm is the last one in the book?
check.why: Psalm 150 is the last psalm. It names many instruments and ends the book with Hallelujah.

check.q: Psalm 100's title calls it a song of what?
check.why: The title of Psalm 100 calls it a psalm of thanksgiving. It tells all the earth to shout with gladness.

lessons.title: Two Lines, One Idea
lessons.mainIdea: Hebrew poetry often says one idea twice in two different ways, and this is called parallelism.
reading: Hebrew poems do not usually rhyme. Instead they do something else. They say an idea once, and then say it again in new words. Scholars call this *parallelism*. The second line is like an echo of the first. It can repeat the idea, add to it, or flip it around.

Look at Psalm 23:2. The first line says God leads the singer to green pastures. The second line says God leads him beside still waters. Two lines, one idea: a safe, calm place. Now look at Psalm 100:2. "Serve the LORD with gladness" and "come before Him with singing" say almost the same thing.

This pattern helps a listener remember. It also helps a reader understand. If one line is hard, the other line explains it. When you read a psalm, try to find the pairs. Ask, "How does the second line echo the first?" This is a key to reading Hebrew poetry.

words.d: a pattern in Hebrew poetry where a second line repeats or echoes the idea of the first
writing that uses pictures and patterns to say something in a strong, short way

look.title: Find the Echo
look.text: Psalm 23:2 has two lines. Line one: the shepherd makes the sheep lie down in green pastures. Line two: the shepherd leads the sheep beside still waters. Now Psalm 137:1 in JPS 1917 says: "By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down, yea, we wept, when we remembered Zion."
look.prompt: In each verse, what is the one idea the two lines share? Try writing your own two-line echo about your favorite place.

check.q: What is parallelism in Hebrew poetry?
choices: Words that rhyme at the end of lines
A second line that echoes the idea of the first
check.why: Parallelism is when a second line repeats, adds to, or flips the idea of the first line. Hebrew poems rarely rhyme.

check.q: In Psalm 23:2, green pastures and still waters share what idea?
check.why: Both lines picture a safe, calm place where the shepherd leads the sheep. That is the shared idea.

check.q: Why does saying an idea twice help a reader?
choices: It makes the psalm longer for singing
If one line is hard, the other line explains it
check.why: The second line explains and echoes the first. Parallelism helps people understand and remember.

lessons.title: A Psalm for Every Day
lessons.mainIdea: Jewish tradition gives each day of the week its own psalm, and the psalms give words to every feeling.
reading: The Psalms hold every kind of feeling. Some are full of joy. Some are full of tears. Psalm 137 was written by people far from home in Babylon. They sat by the river and wept. Other psalms say "help me" or "thank you" or "why?" A psalm that asks for help is called a *lament*.

Jewish tradition gives each day of the week its own psalm. The Mishnah says the Levites sang a different psalm each day in the Temple in Jerusalem. Today many Jews still say that day's psalm in the morning prayers. Sunday's psalm is Psalm 24. The psalm for Shabbat is Psalm 92.

The book of Psalms is also used in the *siddur*, the Jewish prayer book. Many pages of the siddur are made of psalms. On Friday evening, six psalms welcome Shabbat. So the psalms are not only old poems. They are words people use every week.

words.d: a sad song or poem that asks for help or tells about pain
the Jewish prayer book; many of its pages are made of psalms

look.title: The Psalm for Each Day
look.cite: Mishnah Tamid 7:4, as Jewish tradition keeps it in the morning prayers
look.prompt: Which psalm is said on Shabbat? Which two days have psalm numbers that are next to each other?

check.q: What is a lament?
choices: A sad song that asks for help
check.why: A lament is a sad song or poem that asks for help or tells about pain. Psalm 137 is one example.

check.q: What is the siddur?
check.why: The siddur is the Jewish prayer book. Many of its pages come from the Psalms.

check.q: Which psalm does Jewish tradition say for Shabbat?
check.why: The psalm for Shabbat is Psalm 92. Psalm 24 is for Sunday. Psalm 137 is a lament about Babylon.

lessons.title: Mishlei: Short Wise Sayings
lessons.mainIdea: The book of Proverbs is a collection of short sayings that teach how to live wisely, and tradition connects it with King Solomon.
reading: The book of *Proverbs* comes after Psalms in the Ketuvim. In Hebrew it is called *Mishlei*. A proverb is a short saying that teaches something true about life. The book has 31 chapters full of them. Its first verse names Solomon, David's son. Jewish tradition remembers Solomon as very wise.

One famous proverb says, "A soft answer turneth away wrath." Wrath is a big word for anger. The saying means a gentle reply can calm an angry person. The second line adds that a harsh word makes anger grow. Notice the two lines. Proverbs use parallelism too.

Proverbs are about everyday choices. They talk about telling the truth, working hard, being kind and listening to parents. They say that being *wise* starts with respect for God. Scholars say many of these sayings were used to teach young people long ago. They still get used that way today.

words.d: the book of short wise sayings in the Ketuvim; in Hebrew, Mishlei
the Hebrew name of the book of Proverbs
good at knowing what is true and what is right to do

look.title: A Soft Answer
look.text: A soft answer turneth away wrath; but a grievous word stirreth up anger.
look.cite: Proverbs 15:1, The Holy Scriptures, Jewish Publication Society, 1917
look.prompt: Think of a time someone was angry with you. What would a "soft answer" sound like? What would a "grievous word" sound like?

check.q: What is a proverb?
choices: A long story about a king
A short saying that teaches something true about life
check.why: A proverb is a short wise saying. The book of Proverbs holds hundreds of them in 31 chapters.

check.q: Which king does Jewish tradition connect with the book of Proverbs?
check.why: The first verse of Proverbs names Solomon, David's son. Tradition remembers Solomon as very wise.

check.q: According to Proverbs 15:1, what does a soft answer do?
check.why: Proverbs 15:1 says a soft answer turns away wrath. A harsh word stirs up anger instead.

lessons.title: Wisdom Is a Tree of Life
lessons.mainIdea: Proverbs pictures wisdom as a woman calling in the street and as a tree of life, and Jewish prayer still uses these words.
reading: Proverbs likes pictures. In chapter 8, *wisdom* is a woman standing at the city gate. She calls out to everyone who passes by. She says her words are better than silver and gold. The writer wants young people to listen to her, not to foolish friends.

In chapter 3, wisdom is a tree. "She is a tree of life to them that lay hold upon her." The same chapter says her ways are ways of pleasantness and her paths are peace. Jewish tradition sings these lines when the Torah scroll is put back in the ark. So the words of Proverbs are sung in synagogues every week.

Proverbs ends with a poem about a strong and kind woman. She works, she gives to the poor, and she speaks with wisdom. Many Jewish families sing this poem at the Shabbat table on Friday night. It is called *Eshet Chayil*, "a woman of valor."

words.d: knowing what is true and what is right, and choosing to do it
"a woman of valor," the poem at the end of Proverbs; many families sing it on Friday night

look.title: Ways of Pleasantness
look.text: Her ways are ways of pleasantness, and all her paths are peace.
look.cite: Proverbs 3:17, The Holy Scriptures, Jewish Publication Society, 1917
look.prompt: "Her" means wisdom. If wisdom is a road, what would walking on it look like in a classroom?

check.q: In Proverbs 3, wisdom is pictured as what?
check.why: Proverbs 3:18 calls wisdom a tree of life. Chapter 8 pictures her as a woman calling at the gate.

check.q: When do many Jewish families sing Eshet Chayil?
choices: At the Shabbat table on Friday night
On the first day of school
check.why: Eshet Chayil, the poem at the end of Proverbs, is sung by many families on Friday night.

check.q: When are the words "her ways are ways of pleasantness" sung in the synagogue?
choices: When the Torah is put back in the ark
check.why: Jewish tradition sings Proverbs 3:17–18 when the Torah scroll is returned to the ark.

sections.title: Hard Questions and a Love Song

lessons.title: Job Asks Why
lessons.mainIdea: The book of Job tells of a good man who loses everything and asks why bad things happen to good people.
reading: The book of *Job* is different from Psalms and Proverbs. It tells a story, and then it argues. Job is a good man in a land called Uz. He is rich and kind. Then, in one day, he loses his animals, his servants and his children. Later he gets very sick.

Job's first words are famous. He says he came into the world with nothing and will leave with nothing. He says the LORD gave and the LORD took away, and he blesses God's name. But as the book goes on, Job begins to ask questions. He asks why this happened. He says he did nothing wrong.

The big question of the book is: why do bad things happen to good people? Jewish tradition has read Job for a very long time. The rabbis of the Talmud argued about who Job was and when he lived. Some said he was not a real person, but a story to teach. The book does not give one easy answer. It lets the reader ask along with Job.

words.d: the book in the Ketuvim about a good man who loses everything and asks why
something you ask because you want to understand

look.title: Job's First Words
look.text: Naked came I out of my mother's womb, and naked shall I return thither; the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD.
look.cite: Job 1:21, The Holy Scriptures, Jewish Publication Society, 1917
look.prompt: Job says these words right after he loses everything. What do they show about how he feels at first? How might a person feel later?

check.q: What is the big question of the book of Job?
choices: Who will be the next king?
Why do bad things happen to good people?
check.why: Job is a good man who loses everything. The book asks why bad things happen to good people.

check.q: Where does the book say Job lived?
check.why: Job 1:1 says Job lived in the land of Uz. Babylon is the setting of Daniel and Psalm 137.

check.q: What did some rabbis of the Talmud say about Job?
choices: That he was not a real person but a story to teach
That he was a king of Israel
check.why: The Talmud records rabbis who argued about Job, and some said he was a teaching story rather than a real person.

lessons.title: Friends, Questions and a Storm
lessons.mainIdea: Job's friends say he must have done wrong, but the book ends with God speaking from a storm and asking Job questions instead of giving easy answers.
reading: Three friends come to sit with Job. Their names are Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar. At first they say nothing for seven days. Then they start to talk. They say Job must have done something wrong. They say bad things only happen to bad people. Job says that is not true.

Most of the book is this argument. It is written as poetry. Job and his friends take turns. The lines use parallelism, just like the Psalms. Job's *argument* is that he is innocent. His friends' argument is that God is fair, so Job must be guilty. A young man named Elihu speaks too.

At the end, the book says God answers Job out of a *whirlwind*, a big storm. God does not explain why Job suffered. Instead God asks Job questions. Where were you when the earth was made? Can you feed the lions? Job says he has spoken about things too big for him. Then the story says Job's life is made new.

words.d: reasons given to show that an idea is right
a strong spinning storm; in Job, the storm from which God speaks

look.title: Questions From the Storm
look.text: Job 38:4 in JPS 1917: "Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth? Declare, if thou hast understanding." Job asked, "Why did this happen to me?" The voice from the storm does not answer that. It asks Job questions about the sea, the stars, the rain and wild animals.
look.prompt: Why might a book answer a hard question with more questions? Do you think Job got what he wanted? Explain.

check.q: What do Job's three friends say about his troubles?
choices: That Job must have done something wrong
That Job should move to Babylon
check.why: Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar say bad things only happen to bad people, so Job must be guilty. Job disagrees.

check.q: How does the book say God speaks to Job at the end?
check.why: Job 38 says God answers Job out of the whirlwind, a great storm, with questions.

check.q: What does the voice from the storm do?
choices: Tells Job to build a boat
Asks Job questions about the world
check.why: The voice asks Job about the earth, the sea and wild animals. It does not explain his suffering.

lessons.title: The Song of Songs
lessons.mainIdea: The Song of Songs is a love poem full of gardens and springtime, and Jewish tradition reads it on Passover.
reading: The *Song of Songs* is a short book of eight chapters. In Hebrew it is *Shir HaShirim*. Its first verse connects it with Solomon. It is a poem about two people who love each other. They call to each other through gardens and vineyards. They talk about flowers, doves, apples and the spring.

One famous part says that the winter is past and the rain is over. The flowers appear and the time of singing has come. Because it talks about spring, Jewish tradition reads this book on *Passover*. Passover is the spring holiday that remembers leaving Egypt.

The rabbis asked why a love poem is in the Bible. Rabbi Akiva, a teacher long ago, said all the Writings are holy, but the Song of Songs is the holiest of all. Jewish tradition reads the love in the poem as the love between God and the people of Israel. Other readers read it as a poem about human love. Both readings have a long history.

words.d: a short love poem in the Ketuvim, full of gardens and spring; in Hebrew, Shir HaShirim
the spring holiday that remembers the Israelites leaving Egypt; the Song of Songs is read then

look.title: The Winter Is Past
look.text: The poem says the winter is past and the rain is over and gone. Flowers appear on the earth, the time of singing has come, and the voice of the turtledove is heard in the land.
look.cite: Song of Songs 2:11–12, The Holy Scriptures, Jewish Publication Society, 1917
look.prompt: List the signs of spring in these lines. Why would a spring poem fit a spring holiday like Passover?

check.q: On which holiday does Jewish tradition read the Song of Songs?
check.why: The Song of Songs is full of spring, so it is read on Passover, the spring holiday.

check.q: What did Rabbi Akiva say about the Song of Songs?
choices: That it should be left out of the Bible
That it is the holiest of all the Writings
That it is a book of laws
check.why: Tradition records Rabbi Akiva saying all the Writings are holy, but the Song of Songs is the holiest of all.

check.q: How does Jewish tradition often read the love in the Song of Songs?
choices: As a war between two kings
As the love between God and the people of Israel
check.why: Jewish tradition reads the poem's love as the bond between God and Israel. Others read it as a poem about human love.

review.q: Which book comes first in the Ketuvim?
review.why: Psalms is the first book of the Ketuvim, the Writings. Proverbs and Job follow it.

review.q: Psalm 23 pictures God as a shepherd. What does the shepherd do in the psalm?
choices: Leads the sheep to green fields and quiet water
Builds a wall around the city
review.why: Psalm 23 says the shepherd leads to green pastures and still waters and walks through the dark valley.

review.q: "A soft answer turneth away wrath" comes from which book?
review.why: This saying is Proverbs 15:1. Proverbs, or Mishlei, is the book of short wise sayings.

choices: Rhyming words at the end of a line
Reading a scroll from right to left
A second line that echoes the first line's idea
A song with drums and cymbals
review.why: Parallelism is the pattern where a second line repeats or echoes the idea of the first. Hebrew poems use it often.

review.q: Which book asks why bad things happen to good people?
review.why: Job is a good man who loses everything. His book asks why, and his friends argue with him.

review.q: Which word ends Psalm 150 and means "praise the LORD"?
review.why: Hallelujah means "praise the LORD." Tehillim is the name of the book; Mishlei is Proverbs.

review.q: Which book is read on Passover because it is full of spring?
review.why: The Song of Songs talks about flowers and the end of winter, so it is read on Passover.

review.q: The poem Eshet Chayil, "a woman of valor," comes at the end of which book?
review.why: Eshet Chayil is the poem in Proverbs 31. Many families sing it on Friday night.
